entries.e478355b35cf84b529e2e24b826347020c130291: <div sID="gen17399" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Jer.10" sID="Jer.10"/> <div eID="gen17399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17400" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17401" type="x-p"/> We may conjecture that the prophecy of this chapter was delivered after the first captivity, in the time of Jeconiah or Jehoiachin, when many were carried away to Babylon; for it has a double reference:—I. To those that were carried away into the land of the Chaldeans, a country notorious above any other for idolatry and superstition; and they are here cautioned against the infection of the place, not to learn the way of the heathen (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.1-Jer.10.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), for their astrology and idolatry are both foolish things (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.3-Jer.10.5">ver. 3-5</reference>), and the worshippers of idols brutish, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.8-Jer.10.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. So it will appear in the day of their visitation, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.14-Jer.10.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. They are likewise exhorted to adhere firmly to the God of Israel, for there is none like him, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.6-Jer.10.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. He is the true God, lives for ever, and has the government of the world (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.10-Jer.10.13">ver. 10-13</reference>), and his people are happy in him, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.16">ver. 16</reference>. II. To those that yet remained in their own land. They are cautioned against security, and told to expect distress (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.17-Jer.10.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>) and that by a foreign enemy, which God would bring upon them for their sin, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.20-Jer.10.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. This calamity the prophet laments (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.19">ver. 19</reference>) and prays for the mitigation of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.23-Jer.10.25">ver. 23-25</reference>.
entries.228c7862d2059de51f5cec509d136486af4e88b8: <div eID="gen17401" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17400" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Solemn Charge to Israel; The Folly of Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17402" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear ye the word which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> speaketh unto you, O house of Israel: <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the customs of the people <hi type="italic">are</hi> vain: for <hi type="italic">one</hi> cutteth a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman, with the axe. <hi type="super">4</hi> They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it move not. <hi type="super">5</hi> They <hi type="italic">are</hi> upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also <hi type="italic">is it</hi> in them to do good. <hi type="super">6</hi> Forasmuch as <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> great, and thy name <hi type="italic">is</hi> great in might. <hi type="super">7</hi> Who would not fear thee, O King of nations? for to thee doth it appertain: forasmuch as among all the wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like unto thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> But they are altogether brutish and foolish: the stock <hi type="italic">is</hi> a doctrine of vanities. <hi type="super">9</hi> Silver spread into plates is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the workman, and of the hands of the founder: blue and purple <hi type="italic">is</hi> their clothing: they <hi type="italic">are</hi> all the work of cunning <hi type="italic">men.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the true God, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the living God, and an everlasting king: at his wrath the earth shall tremble, and the nations shall not be able to abide his indignation. <hi type="super">11</hi> Thus shall ye say unto them, The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, <hi type="italic">even</hi> they shall perish from the earth, and from under these heavens. <hi type="super">12</hi> He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his discretion. <hi type="super">13</hi> When he uttereth his voice, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a multitude of waters in the heavens, and he causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth; he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures. <hi type="super">14</hi> Every man is brutish in <hi type="italic">his</hi> knowledge: every founder is confounded by the graven image: for his molten image <hi type="italic">is</hi> falsehood, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no breath in them. <hi type="super">15</hi> They <hi type="italic">are</hi> vanity, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the work of errors: in the time of their visitation they shall perish. <hi type="super">16</hi> The portion of Jacob <hi type="italic">is</hi> not like them: for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the former of all <hi type="italic">things;</hi> and Israel <hi type="italic">is</hi> the rod of his inheritance: The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name. <div eID="gen17402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17403" type="x-p"/> The prophet Isaiah, when he prophesied of the captivity in Babylon, added warnings against idolatry and largely exposed the sottishness of idolaters, not only because the temptations in Babylon would be in danger of drawing the Jews there to idolatry, but because the afflictions in Babylon were designed to cure them of their idolatry. Thus the prophet Jeremiah here arms people against the idolatrous usages and customs of the heathen, not only for the use of those that had gone to Babylon, but of those also that staid behind, that being convinced and reclaimed, by the word of God, the rod might be prevented; and it is <hi type="italic">written for our learning.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen17403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17404" type="x-p"/> I. A solemn charge given to the people of God not to conform themselves to the ways and customs of the heathen. Let the house of Israel hear and receive this word from the God of Israel: "<hi type="italic">Learn not the way of the heathen,</hi> do not approve of it, no, nor think indifferently concerning it, much less imitate it or accustom yourselves to it. Let not any of their customs steal in among you (as they are apt to do insensibly) nor mingle themselves with your religion." Note, It ill becomes those that are taught of God to <hi type="italic">learn the way of the heathen,</hi> and to think of worshipping the true God with such rites and ceremonies as they used in the worship of their false gods. See <reference osisRef="Deut.12.29-Deut.12.31">Deut. xii. 29-31</reference>. It was the way of the heathen to worship the host of heaven, the sun, moon, and stars; to them they gave divine honours, and from them they expected divine favours, and therefore, according as <hi type="italic">the signs of heaven</hi> were, whether they were auspicious or ominous, they thought themselves countenanced or discountenanced by their deities, which made them observe those signs, the eclipses of the sun and moon, the conjunctions and oppositions of the planets, and all the unusual phenomena of the celestial globe, with a great deal of anxiety and trembling. Business was stopped if any thing occurred that was thought to bode ill; if it did but thunder on their left hand, they were almost as if they had been thunderstruck. Now God would not have his people to be <hi type="italic">dismayed at the signs of heaven,</hi> to reverence the stars as deities, nor to frighten themselves with any prognostications grounded upon them. Let them fear the God of heaven, and keep up a reverence of his providence, and then they need not be <hi type="italic">dismayed at the signs of heaven,</hi> for the <hi type="italic">stars in their courses</hi> fight not against any that are at peace with God. The heathen are dismayed at these signs, for they know no better; but let not the <hi type="italic">house of Israel,</hi> that are taught of God, be so. <div eID="gen17404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17405" type="x-p"/> II. Divers good reasons given to enforce this charge. <div eID="gen17405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17406" type="x-p"/> 1. The way of the heathen is very ridiculous and absurd, and is condemned even by the dictates of right reason, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.3">v. 3</reference>. The statutes and ordinances of the heathen are vanity itself; they cannot stand the test of a rational disquisition. This is again and again insisted upon here, as it was by Isaiah. The Chaldeans valued themselves upon their wisdom, in which they thought that they excelled all their neighbours; but the prophet here shows that they, and all others that worshipped idols and expected help and relief from them, were brutish and sottish, and had not common sense. (1.) Consider what the idol is that is worshipped. It was a <hi type="italic">tree cut out of the forest</hi> originally. It was fitted up by <hi type="italic">the hands of the workman,</hi> squared, and sawed, and worked into shape; see <reference osisRef="Isa.44.12">Isa. xliv. 12</reference>, &c. But, after all, it was but the stock of a tree, fitter to make a gate-post of than any thing else. But, to hide the wood, <hi type="italic">they deck it with silver and gold,</hi> they gild or lacquer it, or they deck it with gold and silver lace, or cloth of tissue. <hi type="italic">They fasten it</hi> to its place, which they themselves have assigned it, <hi type="italic">with nails and hammers,</hi> that it fall not, nor be thrown down, nor stolen away, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.4">v. 4</reference>. The image is made straight enough, and it cannot be denied but that the workman did his part, for it <hi type="italic">is upright as the palm-tree</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.5">v. 5</reference>); it looks stately, and stands up as if it were going to speak to you, but it <hi type="italic">cannot speak;</hi> it is a poor dumb creature; nor can it take one step towards your relief. If there be any occasion for it to shift its place, it must be carried in procession, for it <hi type="italic">cannot go.</hi> Very fitly does the admonition come in here, "<hi type="italic">Be not afraid of them,</hi> any more than of the signs of heaven; be not afraid of incurring their displeasure, for <hi type="italic">they can do no evil;</hi> be not afraid of forfeiting their favour, <hi type="italic">for neither is it in them to do good.</hi> If you think to mend the matter by mending the materials of which the idol is made, you deceive yourselves. Idols of gold and silver are an unworthy to be worshipped as wooden gods. <hi type="italic">The stock is a doctrine of vanities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.10.8">v. 8</reference>. It teaches lies, teaches lies concerning God. It is <hi type="italic">an instruction of vanities; it is wood.</hi>" It is probable that the idols of gold and silver had wood underneath for the substratum, and then <hi type="italic">silver spread into plates is brought from Tarshish,</hi> imported from beyond sea, <hi type="italic">and gold from Uphaz,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Phaz,</hi> which is sometimes rendered the <hi type="italic">fine</hi> or <hi type="italic">pure gold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Ps. xxi. 3</reference>. A great deal of art is used, and pains taken, about it. They are not such ordinary mechanics that are employed about these as about the wooden gods, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.3">v. 3</reference>. These are cunning men; it is <hi type="italic">the work of the workman;</hi> the graver must do his part when it has passed through <hi type="italic">the hands of the founder.</hi> Those were but decked here and there with silver and gold; these are silver and gold all over. And, that these gods might be reverenced as kings, <hi type="italic">blue and purple are their clothing,</hi> the colour of royal robes (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.9">v. 9</reference>), which amuses ignorant worshippers, but makes the matter no better. For what is the idol when it is made and when they have made the best they can of it? He tells us (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They are falsehood;</hi> they are not what they pretend to be, but a great cheat put upon the world. They are worshipped as the gods that give us breath and life and sense, whereas they are lifeless senseless things themselves, and <hi type="italic">there is no breath in them;</hi> there is <hi type="italic">no spirit in them</hi> (so the word is); they are not animated, or inhabited, as they are supposed to be, by any <hi type="italic">divine spirit</hi> or <hi type="italic">numen—divinity.</hi> They are so far from being gods that they have not so much as the <hi type="italic">spirit of a beast that goes downward. They are vanity, and the work of errors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.10.15">v. 15</reference>. Enquire into the use of them and you will find they are vanity; they are good for nothing; no help is to be expected from them nor any confidence put in them. They are a <hi type="italic">deceitful work, works of illusions,</hi> or <hi type="italic">mere mockeries;</hi> so some read the following clause. They <hi type="italic">delude</hi> those that put their trust in them, make fools of them, or, rather, they make fools of themselves. Enquire into the use of them and you will find they are <hi type="italic">the work of errors,</hi> grounded upon the grossest mistakes that ever men who pretended to reason were guilty of. They are the creatures of a deluded fancy; and the errors by which they were produced they propagate among their worshippers. (2.) Infer hence what the idolaters are that worship these idols. (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They are altogether brutish and foolish.</hi> Those that make them are like unto them, senseless and stupid, and there is no spirit in them—no use of reason, else they would never stoop to them, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Every man</hi> that makes or worships idols has become <hi type="italic">brutish in his knowledge,</hi> that is, brutish for want of knowledge, or brutish in that very thing which one would think they should be fully acquainted with; compare <reference osisRef="Jude.1.10">Jude 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">What they know naturally,</hi> what they cannot but know by the light of nature, <hi type="italic">in those things as brute beasts they corrupt themselves.</hi> Though in the works of creation they cannot but see the eternal power and godhead of the Creator, yet they have become <hi type="italic">vain in their imaginations, not liking to retain God in their knowledge.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Rom. i. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">28</reference>. Nay, whereas they thought it a piece of wisdom thus to multiply gods, it really was the greatest folly they could be guilty of. <hi type="italic">The world by wisdom knew not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1 Cor. i. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.22">Rom. i. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Every founder</hi> is himself <hi type="italic">confounded by the graven image;</hi> when he has made it by a mistake he is more and more confirmed in his mistake by it; he is bewildered, bewitched, and cannot disentangle himself from the snare; or it is what he will one time or other be ashamed of. <div eID="gen17406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17407" type="x-p"/> 2. The God of Israel is the one only living and true God, and those that have him for their God need not make their application to any other; nay, to set up any other in competition with him is the greatest affront and injury that can be done him. Let the house of Israel cleave to the God of Israel and serve and worship him only, for, <div eID="gen17407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17408" type="x-p"/> (1.) He is a non-such. Whatever men may set in competition with him, there is none to be compared with him. The prophet turns from speaking with the utmost disdain of the idols of the heathen (as well he might) to speak with the most profound and awful reverence of the God of Israel (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.6-Jer.10.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Forasmuch as there is none like unto thee, O Lord!</hi> none of all the heroes which the heathen have deified and make such ado about," the dead men of whom they made dead images, and whom they worshipped. "Some were deified and adored for their wisdom; but, <hi type="italic">among all the wise men of the nations,</hi> the greatest philosophers or statesmen, as Apollo or Hermes, <hi type="italic">there is none like thee.</hi> Others were deified and adored for their dominion; but, <hi type="italic">in all their royalty</hi>" (so it may be read), "among all their kings, as Saturn and Jupiter, <hi type="italic">there is none like unto thee.</hi>" What is the glory of a man that invented a useful art or founded a flourishing kingdom (and these were grounds sufficient among the heathen to entitle a man to an apotheosis) compared with the glory of him that is the Creator of the world and that <hi type="italic">forms the spirit of man within him?</hi> What is the glory of the greatest prince or potentate, compared with the glory of him whose <hi type="italic">kingdom rules over all?</hi> He acknowledges (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">O Lord! thou art great,</hi> infinite and immense, and <hi type="italic">thy name is great in might;</hi> thou hast all power, and art known to have it. Men's name is often beyond their might; they are thought to be greater than they are; but God's <hi type="italic">name is great,</hi> and no greater than he really is. And therefore <hi type="italic">who would not fear thee, O King of nations?</hi> Who would not choose to worship such a God as this, that can do every thing, rather than such dead idols as the heathen worship, that can do nothing? Who would not be afraid of offending or forsaking a God whose name is so <hi type="italic">great in might?</hi> Which of all the nations, if they understood their interests aright, <hi type="italic">would not fear him</hi> who is the <hi type="italic">King of nations?</hi> Note, There is an admirable decency and congruity in the worshipping of God only. It is fit that he who is God alone should alone be served, that he who is Lord of all should be served by all, that he who is great should be greatly feared and greatly praised. <div eID="gen17408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17409" type="x-p"/> (2.) His verity is as evident as the idol's vanity, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10">v. 10</reference>. They are the work of men's hands, and therefore nothing is more plain than that it is a jest to worship them, if that may be called a jest which is so great an indignity to him that made us: <hi type="italic">But the Lord is the true God,</hi> the God of truth; he is God in truth. <hi type="italic">God Jehovah is truth;</hi> he is not a counterfeit and pretender, as they are, but is really what he has revealed himself to be; he is one we may depend upon, in whom and by whom we cannot be deceived. [1.] Look upon him as he is in himself, and he is <hi type="italic">the living God.</hi> He is life itself, has life in himself, and is the fountain of life to all the creatures. The gods of the heathen are dead things, worthless and useless, but ours is a living God, and hath immortality. [2.] Look upon him with relation to his creatures, he is a <hi type="italic">King,</hi> and absolute monarch, over them all, is their owner and ruler, has an incontestable right both to command them and dispose of them. As a king, he protects the creatures, provides for their welfare, and preserves peace among them. He is <hi type="italic">an everlasting king.</hi> The counsels of his kingdom were from everlasting and the continuance of it will be to everlasting. He is a <hi type="italic">King of eternity.</hi> The idols whom they call their kings are but of yesterday, and will soon be abolished; and the kings of the earth, that set them up to be worshipped, will themselves be in the dust shortly; but <hi type="italic">the Lord shall reign for ever, thy God, O Zion! unto all generations.</hi> <div eID="gen17409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17410" type="x-p"/> (3.) None knows the power of his anger. Let us stand in awe, and not dare to provoke him by giving that glory to another which is due to him alone; for <hi type="italic">at his wrath the earth shall tremble,</hi> even the strongest and stoutest of the kings of the earth; nay, the earth, firmly as it is fixed, when he pleases is made to quake and the rocks to tremble, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.32">Ps. civ. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6 Hab.3.10">Hab. iii. 6, 10</reference>. Though the nations should join together to contend with him, and unite their force, yet they would be found utterly unable not only to resist, but even <hi type="italic">to abide his indignation.</hi> Not only can they not make head against it, for it would overcome them, but they cannot bear up under it, for it would overload them, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.7-Ps.76.8">Ps. lxxvi. 7, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.6">Nah. i. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen17410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17411" type="x-p"/> (4.) He is the God of nature, the fountain of all being; and all the powers of nature are at his command and disposal, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.12-Jer.10.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. The God we worship is he that made the heavens and the earth, and has a sovereign dominion over both; so that his <hi type="italic">invisible things</hi> are manifested and proved in the <hi type="italic">things that are seen.</hi> [1.] If we look back, we find that the whole world owed its origin to him as its first cause. It was a common saying even among the Greeks—<hi type="italic">He that sets up to be another god ought first to make another world.</hi> While the heathen worship gods that they made, we worship the God that made us and all things. <hi type="italic">First, The earth</hi> is a body of vast bulk, has valuable treasures in its bowels and more valuable fruit on its surface. It and them he has <hi type="italic">made by his power;</hi> and it is by no less than an infinite power that it <hi type="italic">hangs upon nothing,</hi> as it does (<reference osisRef="Job.26.7">Job xxvi. 7</reference>)— <hi type="italic">ponderibus librata suis—poised by its own weight. Secondly, The world,</hi> the habitable part of the earth, is admirably fitted for the use and service of man, and <hi type="italic">he hath established it</hi> so <hi type="italic">by his wisdom,</hi> so that it continues serviceable in constant changes and yet a continual stability from one generation to another. Therefore both the earth and the world are his, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Ps. xxiv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly, The heavens</hi> are wonderfully <hi type="italic">stretched out</hi> to an incredible extent, and it is <hi type="italic">by his discretion</hi> that they are so, and that the motions of the heavenly bodies are directed for the benefit of this lower world. These <hi type="italic">declare his glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.1">Ps. xix. 1</reference>), and oblige us to declare it, and not give that glory to the heavens which is due to him that made them. [2.] If we look up, we see his providence to be a continued creation (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he uttereth his voice</hi> (gives the word of command) <hi type="italic">there is a multitude of waters in the heavens,</hi> which are poured out on the earth, whether for judgment or mercy, as he intends them. When he utters his voice in the thunder, immediately there follow thunder-showers, in which there are a multitude of waters; and those come with <hi type="italic">a noise,</hi> as the margin reads it; and we read of the <hi type="italic">noise of abundance of rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.41">1 Kings xviii. 41</reference>. Nay, there are wonders done daily in the kingdom of nature without noise: <hi type="italic">He causes the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth,</hi> from all parts of the earth, even the most remote, and chiefly those that lie next the sea. All the earth pays the tribute of vapours, because all the earth receives the blessing of rain. And thus the moisture in the universe, like the money in a kingdom and the blood in the body, is continually circulating for the good of the whole. Those vapours produce wonders, for of them are formed <hi type="italic">lightnings for the rain,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the winds</hi> which God from time to time <hi type="italic">brings forth out of his treasures,</hi> as there is occasion for them, directing them all in such measure and for such use as he thinks fit, as payments are made out of the treasury. All the meteors are so ready to serve God's purposes that he seems to have treasures of them, that cannot be exhausted and may at any time be drawn from, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>. God glories in the treasures he has of these, <reference osisRef="Job.38.22-Job.38.23">Job xxxviii. 22, 23</reference>. This God can do; but which of the idols of the heathen can do the like? Note, There is no sort of weather but what furnishes us with a proof and instance of the wisdom and power of the great Creator. <div eID="gen17411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17412" type="x-p"/> (5.) This God is Israel's God in covenant, and the felicity of every Israelite indeed. Therefore let the house of Israel cleave to him, and not forsake him to embrace idols; for, if they do, they certainly change for the worse, for (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">the portion of Jacob is not like them;</hi> their rock is not as our rock (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.31">Deut. xxxii. 31</reference>), nor ours like their mole-hills. Note, [1.] Those that have the Lord for their God have a full and complete happiness in him. The <hi type="italic">God of Jacob</hi> is the <hi type="italic">portion of Jacob;</hi> he is his all, and in him he has enough and needs no more in this world nor the other. In him we have a worthy portion, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Ps. xvi. 5</reference>. [2.] If we have entire satisfaction and complacency in God as our portion, he will have a gracious delight in us as his people, whom he owns as <hi type="italic">the rod of his inheritance,</hi> his possession and treasure, with whom he dwells and by whom he is served and honoured. [3.] It is the unspeakable comfort of all the Lord's people that he who is their God is <hi type="italic">the former of all things,</hi> and therefore is able to do all that for them, and give all that to them, which they stand in need of. Their <hi type="italic">help stands in his name who made heaven and earth.</hi> And he is the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> of all the hosts in heaven and earth, has them all at his command, and will command them into the service of his people when there is occasion. This is the name by which they know him, which they first give him the glory of and then take to themselves the comfort of. [4.] Herein God's people are happy above all other people, happy indeed, <hi type="italic">bona si sua norint—did they but know their blessedness.</hi> The gods which the heathen pride, and please, and so portion themselves in, are vanity and a lie; but <hi type="italic">the portion of Jacob is not like them.</hi> <div eID="gen17412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17413" type="x-p"/> 3. The prophet, having thus compared the gods of the heathen with the God of Israel (between whom there is no comparison), reads the doom, the certain doom, of all those pretenders, and directs the Jews, in God's name, to read it to the worshippers of idols, though they were their lords and masters (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus shall you say unto them</hi> (and the God you serve will bear you out in saying it), <hi type="italic">The gods which have not made the heavens and the earth</hi> (and therefore are no gods, but usurpers of the honour due to him only who did make heaven and earth) <hi type="italic">shall perish,</hi> perish of course, because they are vanity—perish by his righteous sentence, because they are rivals with him. As gods they shall perish <hi type="italic">from off the earth</hi> (even all those things <hi type="italic">on earth beneath</hi> which they make gods of) <hi type="italic">and from under these heavens,</hi> even all those things in the firmament of heaven, under the highest heavens, which are deified, according to the distribution in the second commandment. These words in the original are not in the Hebrew, like all the rest, but in the Chaldee dialect, that the Jews in captivity might have this ready to say to the Chaldeans in their own language when they tempted them to idolatry: "Do you press us to worship your gods? We will never do that; for," (1.) "They are counterfeit deities; they are no gods, for they <hi type="italic">have not made the heavens and the earth,</hi> and therefore are not entitled to our homage, nor are we indebted to them either for the products of the earth or the influences of heaven, as we are to the God of Israel." The primitive Christians would say, when they were urged to worship such a god, <hi type="italic">Let him make a world and he shall be my god.</hi> While we have him to worship who made heaven and earth, it is very absurd to worship any other. (2.) "They are condemned deities. They <hi type="italic">shall perish;</hi> the time shall come when they shall be no more respected as they are now, but shall be buried in oblivion, and they and their worshippers shall sink together. The earth shall no longer bear them; the heavens shall no longer cover them; but both shall abandon them." It is repeated (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">In the time of their visitation</hi> they shall perish. When God comes to reckon with idolaters he will make them weary of their idols, and glad to be rid of them. They shall <hi type="italic">cast them to the moles and to the bats,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa. ii. 20</reference>. Whatever runs against God and religion will be run down at last.
entries.7740237146e975825308eb9fe2a4637bc6a3c1b0: <div eID="gen17413" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Lamentation of Judah; Sovereignty of Divine Providence; Prophetic Imprecations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  606.)</title> <div sID="gen17414" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Gather up thy wares out of the land, O inhabitant of the fortress. <hi type="super">18</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this once, and will distress them, that they may find <hi type="italic">it so.</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> Woe is me for my hurt! my wound is grievous: but I said, Truly this <hi type="italic">is</hi> a grief, and I must bear it. <hi type="super">20</hi> My tabernacle is spoiled, and all my cords are broken: my children are gone forth of me, and they <hi type="italic">are</hi> not: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none to stretch forth my tent any more, and to set up my curtains. <hi type="super">21</hi> For the pastors are become brutish, and have not sought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : therefore they shall not prosper, and all their flocks shall be scattered. <hi type="super">22</hi> Behold, the noise of the bruit is come, and a great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah desolate, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a den of dragons. <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , I know that the way of man <hi type="italic">is</hi> not in himself: <hi type="italic">it is</hi> not in man that walketh to direct his steps. <hi type="super">24</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing. <hi type="super">25</hi> Pour out thy fury upon the heathen that know thee not, and upon the families that call not on thy name: for they have eaten up Jacob, and devoured him, and consumed him, and have made his habitation desolate. <div eID="gen17414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17415" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen17415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17416" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet threatens, in God's name, the approaching ruin of Judah and Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.17-Jer.10.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. The Jews that continued in their own land, after some were carried into captivity, were very secure; they thought themselves <hi type="italic">inhabitants of a fortress;</hi> their country was their strong hold, and, in their own conceit, impregnable; but they are here told to think of leaving it: they must prepare to go after their brethren, and pack up their effects in expectation of it: "<hi type="italic">Gather up thy wares out of the land;</hi> contract your affairs, and bring them into as small a compass as you can. <hi type="italic">Arise, depart, this is not your rest,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mic. ii. 10</reference>. Let not what you have lie scattered, for the Chaldeans will be upon you again, to be the executioners of the sentence God has passed upon you (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold, I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this once;</hi> they have hitherto dropped out, by a few at a time, but one captivity more shall make a thorough riddance, and they shall be slung out as a stone out of a sling, so easily, so thoroughly shall they be cast out; nothing of them shall remain. They shall be thrown out with violence, and driven to a place at a great distance off, in a little time." See this comparison used to signify an utter destruction, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1 Sam. xxv. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">Yet once more</hi> God will shake their land, and <hi type="italic">shake the wicked out of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">Heb. xii. 26</reference>. He adds, <hi type="italic">And I will distress them, that they may find it so.</hi> He will not only throw them out hence (that he may do and yet they may be easy elsewhere); but, whithersoever they go, trouble shall follow them; they shall be continually perplexed and straitened, and at a loss within themselves: and who or what can make those easy whom God <hi type="italic">will distress,</hi> whom he will distress <hi type="italic">that they may find it so,</hi> that they may feel that which they would not believe? They were often told of the weight of God's wrath and their utter inability to make head against it, or bear up under it. They were told that their sin would be their ruin, and they would not regard nor credit what was told them; but now <hi type="italic">they shall find it so;</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> God will pursue them with his judgments, <hi type="italic">that they may find it so,</hi> and be forced to acknowledge it. Note, sooner or later sinners will find it just as the word of God has represented things to them, and no better, and that the threatenings were not bugbears. <div eID="gen17416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17417" type="x-p"/> II. He brings in the people sadly lamenting their calamities (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Woe is me for my hurt!</hi> Some make this the prophet's own lamentation, not for himself, but for the calamities and desolations of his country. He mourned for those that would not be persuaded to mourn for themselves; and, since there were none that had so much sense as to join with them, he weeps in secret, and cries out, <hi type="italic">Woe is me!</hi> In mournful times it becomes us to be of a mournful spirit. But it may be taken as the language of the people, considered as a body, and therefore speaking as a single person. The prophet puts into their mouths the words they <hi type="italic">should</hi> say; whether they would say them or no, they should have cause to say them. Some among them would thus bemoan themselves, and all of them, at last, would be forced to do it. 1. They lament that the affliction is very great, and it is very hard to them to bear it, the more hard because they had not been used to trouble and now did not expect it: "<hi type="italic">Woe is me for my hurt,</hi> not for what I fear, but for what I feel;" for they are not, as some are, worse frightened than hurt. Nor is it a slight hurt, but <hi type="italic">a wound,</hi> a wound that is <hi type="italic">grievous,</hi> very painful, and very threatening. 2. That there is no remedy but patience. They cannot help themselves, but must sit still, and abide it: <hi type="italic">But I said,</hi> when I was about to complain of my wound, To what purpose is it to complain? <hi type="italic">This is a grief, and I must bear it</hi> as well as I can. This is the language rather of a sullen than of a gracious submission, of a patience per force, not a patience by principle. When I am in affliction I should say, "This is an evil, and I will bear it, because it is the will of God that I should, because his wisdom has appointed this for me and his grace will make it work for good to me." This is <hi type="italic">receiving evil</hi> at the hand of God, <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">Job ii. 10</reference>. But to say, "This is an evil, <hi type="italic">and I must bear it,</hi> because I cannot help it," is but a brutal patience, and argues a want of those good thoughts of God which we should always have, even under our afflictions, saying, not only, God can and will do what he pleases, but, <hi type="italic">Let him do what he pleases.</hi> 3. That the country was quite ruined and wasted (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">My tabernacle is spoiled.</hi> Jerusalem, though a strong city, now proves as weak and moveable as a tabernacle or tent, when it is taken down, and <hi type="italic">all its cords,</hi> that should keep it together, are <hi type="italic">broken.</hi> Or by the tabernacle here may be meant the temple, the sanctuary, which at first was but a tabernacle, and is now called so, as then it was sometimes called a temple. Their church is ruined, and all the supports of it fail. It was a general destruction of church and state, city and country, and there were none to repair these desolations. "<hi type="italic">My children have gone forth of me;</hi> some have fled, others are slain, others carried into captivity, so that as to me, <hi type="italic">they are not;</hi> I am likely to be an outcast, and to perish for want of shelter; for <hi type="italic">there is none to stretch forth my tent any more,</hi> none of my children that used to do it for me, <hi type="italic">none to set up my curtains,</hi> none to do me any service." <hi type="italic">Jerusalem has none to guide her of all her sons,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.18">Isa. li. 18</reference>. 4. That the rulers took no care, nor any proper measures, for the redress of their grievances and the re-establishing of heir ruined state (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">The pastors have become brutish.</hi> When the tents, the shepherds' tents, were spoiled (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.20">v. 20</reference>), it concerned the shepherds to look after them; but they were foolish shepherds. Their kings and princes had no regard at all for the public welfare, seemed to have no sense of the desolations of the land, but were quite besotted and infatuated. The priests, the pastors of God's tabernacle, did a great deal towards the ruin of religion, but nothing towards the repair of it. They are <hi type="italic">brutish</hi> indeed, for <hi type="italic">they have not sought the Lord;</hi> they have neither made their peace with him nor their prayer to him; they had no eye to him and his providence, in their management of affairs; they neither acknowledged the judgment, nor expected the deliverance, to come from his hand. Note, Those are brutish people that do not seek the Lord, that live without prayer, and live without God in the world. Every man is either a saint or a brute. But it is sad indeed with a people when their pastors, that should <hi type="italic">feed them with knowledge and understanding,</hi> are themselves thus brutish. And what comes of it? <hi type="italic">Therefore they shall not prosper;</hi> none of their attempts for the public safety shall succeed. Note, Those cannot expect to prosper who do not by faith and prayer take God along with them in all their ways. And, when the pastors are brutish, what else can be expected but that <hi type="italic">all their flocks</hi> should be <hi type="italic">scattered? For, if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the ditch.</hi> The ruin of a people is often owing to the brutishness of their pastors. 5. That the report of the enemy's approach was very dreadful (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">The noise of the bruit has come,</hi> of the report which at first was but whispered and bruited abroad, as wanting confirmation. It now proves too true: <hi type="italic">A great commotion</hi> arises <hi type="italic">out of the north country,</hi> which threatens to make all <hi type="italic">the cities of Judah desolate and a den of dragons;</hi> for they must all expect to be sacrificed to the avarice and fury of the Chaldean army. And what else can that place expect but to be made a den of dragons which has by sin made itself a den of thieves? <div eID="gen17417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17418" type="x-p"/> III. He turns to God, and addresses himself to him, finding it to little purpose to speak to the people. It is some comfort to poor ministers that, if men will not hear them, God will; and to him they have liberty of access at all times. Let them close their preaching with prayer, as the prophet, and then they shall have no reason to say that they have laboured in vain. <div eID="gen17418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17419" type="x-p"/> 1. The prophet here acknowledges the sovereignty and dominion of the divine Providence, that by it, and not by their own will and wisdom, the affairs both of nations and particular persons are directed and determined, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.23">v. 23</reference>. This is an article of our faith which it is very proper for us to make confession of at the throne of grace when we are complaining of an affliction or suing for a mercy: "<hi type="italic">O Lord, I know,</hi> and believe, <hi type="italic">that the way of man is not in himself;</hi> Nebuchadnezzar did not come of himself against our land, but by the direction of a divine Providence." We cannot of ourselves do any thing for our own relief, unless God work with us and command deliverance for us; for <hi type="italic">it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps,</hi> though he seem in his walking to be perfectly at liberty and to choose his own way. Those that had promised themselves a long enjoyment of their estates and possessions were made to know, by sad experience, when they were thrown out by the Chaldeans, that <hi type="italic">the way of man is not in himself;</hi> he designs which men lay deep, and think well-formed, are dashed to pieces in a moment. We must all apply this to ourselves, and mix faith with it, that we are not at our own disposal, but under a divine direction; the event is often overruled so as to be quite contrary to our intention and expectation. We are not masters of our own way, nor can we think that every thing should be according to our mind; we must therefore refer ourselves to God and acquiesce in his will. Some think that the prophet here mentions this with a design to make this comfortable use of it, that, the way of the Chaldean army being not in themselves, they can do no more than God permits them; he can set bounds to these proud waves, and say, <hi type="italic">Hitherto they shall come, and no further.</hi> And a quieting consideration it is that the most formidable enemies have <hi type="italic">no power against us but what is given them from above.</hi> <div eID="gen17419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17420" type="x-p"/> 2. He deprecates the divine wrath, that it might not fall upon God's Israel, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.24">v. 24</reference>. He speaks not for himself only, but on the behalf of his people: <hi type="italic">O Lord, correct me, but with judgment</hi> (in measure and with moderation, and in wisdom, no more than is necessary for driving out of the foolishness that is bound up in our hearts), <hi type="italic">not in thy anger</hi> (how severe soever the correction be, let it come from thy love, and be designed for our good and made to work for good), not to <hi type="italic">bring us to nothing,</hi> but to bring us home to thyself. Let it not be according to the desert of our sins, but according to the design of thy grace. Note, (1.) We cannot pray in faith that we may never be corrected, while we are conscious to ourselves that we need correction and deserve it, and know that as many as God loves he chastens. (2.) The great thing we should dread in affliction is the wrath of God. Say not, Lord, <hi type="italic">do not correct</hi> me, but, Lord, do not correct me <hi type="italic">in anger;</hi> for that will infuse wormwood and gall into the affliction and misery that will <hi type="italic">bring us to nothing.</hi> We may bear the smart of his rod, but we cannot bear the weight of his wrath. <div eID="gen17420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17421" type="x-p"/> 3. He imprecates the divine wrath against the oppressors and persecutors of Israel (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Pour out thy fury upon the heathen that know thee not.</hi> This prayer does not come from a spirit of malice or revenge, nor is it intended to prescribe to God whom he should execute his judgments upon, or in what order; but, (1.) It is an appeal to his justice. As if he had said, "Lord, we are a provoking people; but are there not other nations that are more so? And shall we only be punished? We are thy children, and may expect a fatherly correction; but they are thy enemies, and against them we have reason to think thy indignation should be, not against us." This is God's usual method. The <hi type="italic">cup put into the hands</hi> of God's people is <hi type="italic">full of mixtures,</hi> mixtures of mercy; but the <hi type="italic">dregs of the cup</hi> are reserved for <hi type="italic">the wicked of the earth,</hi> let them <hi type="italic">wring them out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Ps. lxxv. 8</reference>. (2.) It is a prediction of God's judgments upon all the impenitent enemies of his church and kingdom. If <hi type="italic">judgment begin</hi> thus <hi type="italic">at the house of God,</hi> what shall be <hi type="italic">the end of those that obey not his gospel?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1 Pet. iv. 17</reference>. See how the heathen are described, on whom God's fury shall be poured out. [1.] They are strangers to God, and are content to be so. They <hi type="italic">know him not,</hi> nor desire to know him. They are families that live without prayer, that have nothing of religion among them; they <hi type="italic">call not on God's name.</hi> Those that restrain prayer prove that they know not God; for those that know him will seek to him and entreat his favour. [2.] They are persecutors of the people of God and are resolved to be so. <hi type="italic">They have eaten up Jacob</hi> with as much greediness as those that are hungry eat their necessary food; nay, with more, they have <hi type="italic">devoured him, and consumed him, and made his habitation desolate,</hi> that is, the land in which he lives, or the temple of God, which is his habitation among them. Note, What the heathen, in their rage and malice, do against the people of God, though therein he makes use of them as the instruments of his correction, yet he will, for that, make them the objects of his indignation. This prayer is taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.79.6-Ps.79.7">Ps. lxxix. 6, 7</reference>.  <chapter eID="Jer.10"/> <div eID="gen17421" type="x-p"/>

Contrast between the Idols and Jehovah. The Prophet's Lamentation and Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen17387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9821"/><hi type="bold">1. Israel--</hi>the Jews, the surviving representatives of the nation. <div eID="gen17387" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8077573f8e12dcd3892121adfbd4f65001a44ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9822"/><div sID="gen17388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9822"/>2. Eichorn thinks the reference here to be to some celestial portent which had appeared at that time, causing the Jews' dismay. Probably the reference is general, namely, to the Chaldeans, famed as astrologers, through contact with whom the Jews were likely to fall into the same superstition.<div eID="gen17388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">way--</hi>the precepts or ordinances (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.3">Le 18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.2">Ac 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">signs of heaven--</hi>The Gentiles did not acknowledge a Great First Cause: many thought events depended on the power of the stars, which some, as Plato, thought to be endued with spirit and reason. All heavenly phenomena, eclipses, comets, &c., are included.<div eID="gen17390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one cutteth a tree, &c.--</hi>rather, "It (that which they busy themselves about: a sample of their 'customs') is a tree cut out of the forest" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen17391" type="x-p"/>
entries.412e80dea7e2fb808012ff556f220a0434ae7f92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9823"/><div sID="gen17392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9823"/><hi type="bold">4. fasten ... move not--</hi>that is, that it may stand upright without risk of falling, which the god (!) would do, if left to itself (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.7">Is 41:7</reference>). <div eID="gen17392" type="x-p"/>
entries.526bd31079d686b54083cc265d9631e99bc77c54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9824"/><div sID="gen17393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9824"/><hi type="bold">5. upright--</hi>or, "They are of turned work, resembling a palm tree" [Maurer]. The point of comparison between the idol and the palm is in the pillar-like uprightness of the latter, it having no branches except at the top.<div eID="gen17393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.115.5">Psa 115:5</reference>).<div eID="gen17394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot go--</hi>that is, walk (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.7">Psa 115:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Is 46:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen17395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... do good--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.41.23">Is 41:23</reference>). <div eID="gen17396" type="x-p"/>
entries.13201da4a5e6afa8b9d30b25623ea8e90ec0799e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9825"/><div sID="gen17397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9825"/><hi type="bold">6. none--</hi>literally, "no particle of nothing": nothing whatever; the strongest possible denial (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Ex 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.8">Psa 86:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen17397" type="x-p"/>
entries.569051da2cf284ced21897302fc2b9e987d7a210: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9826"/><div sID="gen17398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9826"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Rev.15.4">Re 15:4</reference>).<div eID="gen17398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to thee doth it appertain--</hi>to Thee it properly belongs, namely, that Thou shouldest be "feared" (taken out of the previous "fear Thee") (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>). He alone is the becoming object of worship. To worship any other is unseemly and an infringement of His inalienable prerogative.<div eID="gen17399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none--</hi>nothing whatever (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.10.6">Jr 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.6">Psa 89:6</reference>). <div eID="gen17400" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d5c8e92acce9eecdbf32acbc372540ac7c66649: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9827"/><div sID="gen17401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9827"/><hi type="bold">8. altogether--</hi>rather, "all alike" [Maurer]. Even the so-called "wise" men (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.7">Jr 10:7</reference>) of the Gentiles are on a level with the brutes and "foolish," namely, because they connive at the popular idolatry (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21-Rom.1.28">Ro 1:21-28</reference>). Therefore, in Daniel and Revelation, the world power is represented under a bestial form. Man divests himself of his true humanity, and sinks to the level of the brute, when he severs his connection with God (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.8">Psa 115:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">Jon 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen17401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stock is a doctrine of vanities--</hi>The stock (put for the worship of all idols whatever, made out of a stock) speaks for itself that the whole theory of idolatry is vanity (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.9-Isa.44.11">Is 44:9-11</reference>). Castalio translates, "the very wood itself confuting the vanity" (of the idol). <div eID="gen17402" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb6c3436327fd209f432069fe9145207c54ce707: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9828"/><div sID="gen17403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9828"/>9. Everything connected with idols is the result of human effort.<div eID="gen17403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Silver spread--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Is 30:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.19">Is 40:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tarshish--</hi>Tartessus, in Spain, famed for precious metals.<div eID="gen17405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Uphaz--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Da 10:5</reference>). As the Septuagint in the Syrian Hexapla in the Margin, Theodotus, the Syrian and Chaldee versions have "Ophir," Gesenius thinks "Uphaz" a colloquial corruption (one letter only being changed) for "Ophir." Ophir, in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.29">Ge 10:29</reference>, is mentioned among Arabian countries. Perhaps Malacca is the country meant, the natives of which still call their gold mines Ophirs. Heeren thinks Ophir the general name for the rich countries of the south, on the Arabian, African, and Indian coasts; just as our term, East Indies.<div eID="gen17406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cunning--</hi>skilful. <div eID="gen17407" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d1608a4c7ee3443ba8dc6363df740a32fe28057: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9829"/><div sID="gen17408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9829"/><hi type="bold">10. true God--</hi>literally, "God Jehovah is truth"; not merely true, that is, veracious, but truth in the reality of His essence, as opposed to the "vanity" or emptiness which all idols are (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.3">Jr 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.15">8, 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2Ch 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Psa 31:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.20">1Jo 5:20</reference>).<div eID="gen17408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">living God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.5.26">Joh 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1Ti 6:17</reference>). He hath life in Himself which no creature has. All else "live in Him" (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.28">Ac 17:28</reference>). In contrast to dead idols.<div eID="gen17409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.10.16">Psa 10:16</reference>). In contrast to the temporary existence of all other objects of worship. <div eID="gen17410" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6c5a6e39dd07aea02bb58f5ed2f7658326d06bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9830"/><div sID="gen17411" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9830"/>11. This verse is in Chaldee, Jeremiah supplying his countrymen with a formula of reply to Chaldee idolaters in the tongue most intelligible to the latter. There may be also derision intended in imitating their barbarous dialect. Rosenmuller objects to this view, that not merely the words put in the mouths of the Israelites, but Jeremiah's own introductory words, "Thus shall ye say to them," are in Chaldee, and thinks it to be a marginal gloss. But it is found in all the oldest versions. It was an old Greek saying: "Whoever thinks himself a god besides the one God, let him make another world" (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.5">Psa 96:5</reference>).<div eID="gen17411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17412" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall perish--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.2.18">Is 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.2">Zec 13:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these heavens--</hi>the speaker pointing to them with his fingers. <div eID="gen17413" type="x-p"/>
entries.05bfd154cf2da92d3e4a43aa7f998593c2b4b8e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9831"/><div sID="gen17414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9831"/>12. Continuation of <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10">Jr 10:10</reference>, after the interruption of the thread of the discourse in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">Jr 10:11</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.5">Psa 136:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen17414" type="x-p"/>
entries.7de377f6e9a46a3fab562db489ba008687292686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9832"/><div sID="gen17415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9832"/>13. Literally, "At the voice of His giving forth," that is, when He thunders. (<reference osisRef="Job.38.34">Job 38:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.29.3-Ps.29.5">Psa 29:3-5</reference>).<div eID="gen17415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waters--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.1.7">Ge 1:7</reference>)--above the firmament; heavy rains accompany thunder.<div eID="gen17416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17417" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vapours ... ascend--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Psa 135:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treasures--</hi>His stores. <div eID="gen17418" type="x-p"/>
entries.0689fd6655f70e75b95c79aab80ec7fe7ffd0ef0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9833"/><div sID="gen17419" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9833"/><hi type="bold">14. in his knowledge--</hi>"is rendered brutish by his skill," namely, in idol-making (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.8">Jr 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.9">9</reference>). Thus the parallel, "confounded by the graven image," corresponds (so <reference osisRef="Jer.51.17">Jr 51:17</reference>). Others not so well translate, "without knowledge," namely, of God (see <reference osisRef="Isa.42.17">Is 42:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">45:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.6">Ho 4:6</reference>). <div eID="gen17419" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2fa53679cec9a4c4b2f5fc3ae68149698e0b9bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9834"/><div sID="gen17420" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9834"/><hi type="bold">15. errors--</hi>deceptions; from a Hebrew root, "to stutter"; then meaning "to mock."<div eID="gen17420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17421" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their visitation they--</hi>When God shall punish the idol-worshippers (namely, by Cyrus), the idols themselves shall be destroyed [Rosenmuller] (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">Jr 10:11</reference>). <div eID="gen17421" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2e0469176dc1754b7950073d45091261aadd27a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9835"/><div sID="gen17422" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9835"/><hi type="bold">16. portion--</hi>from a Hebrew root, "to divide." God is the all-sufficient Good of His people (<reference osisRef="Num.18.20">Nu 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.26">73:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.24">La 3:24</reference>).<div eID="gen17422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not like them--</hi>not like the idols, a vain object of trust (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.31">De 32:31</reference>).<div eID="gen17423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">former of all things--</hi>the Fashioner (as a potter, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">Is 64:8</reference>) of the universe.<div eID="gen17424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rod of his inheritance--</hi>The portion marked off as His inheritance by the measuring rod (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.21">Eze 48:21</reference>). As He is their portion, so are they His portion (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">De 32:9</reference>). A reciprocal tie (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.19">Jr 51:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.2">Psa 74:2</reference>, Margin). Others make "rod" refer to the tribal rod or scepter. <div eID="gen17425" type="x-p"/>
entries.47c3b81076f3b4841679884d8fb1af004143d418: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9836"/><div sID="gen17426" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9836"/><hi type="bold">17. wares--</hi>thine effects or movable goods (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.3">Eze 12:3</reference>). Prepare for migrating as captives to Babylon. The address is to Jerusalem, as representative of the whole people.<div eID="gen17426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inhabitant of the fortress--</hi>rather, "inhabitress of the fortress." Though thou now seemest to inhabit an impregnable fortress, thou shalt have to remove. "The land" is the champaign region opposed to the "fortified" cities. The "fortress" being taken, the whole "land" will share the disaster. Henderson translates, "Gather up thy packages from the ground." Rosenmuller, for "fortress," translates, "siege," that is, the besieged city. The various articles, in this view, are supposed to be lying about in confusion on the ground during the siege. <div eID="gen17427" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1f4227cc64486acd8ae9c4507c9b59a39e14454: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9837"/><div sID="gen17428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9837"/><hi type="bold">18. sling out--</hi>expressing the violence and suddenness of the removal to Babylon. A similar image occurs in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.13">Jr 16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1Sa 25:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.17">Is 22:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">18</reference>.<div eID="gen17428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17429" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at this once--</hi>at this time, now.<div eID="gen17429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">find it so--</hi>find it by experience, that is, feel it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:10</reference>). Michaelis translates, "I will bind them together (as in a sling) that they may reach the goal" (Babylon). English Version is best: "that they may find it so as I have said" (<reference osisRef="Num.23.19">Nu 23:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17430" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fdb14ca19f918b3839d9e3940b99a9c4d522866: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9838"/><div sID="gen17431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9838"/>19. Judea bewails its calamity.<div eID="gen17431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wound--</hi>the stroke I suffer under.<div eID="gen17432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I must bear--</hi>not humble submission to God's will (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mi 7:9</reference>), but sullen impenitence. Or, rather, it is prophetical of their ultimate acknowledgment of their guilt as the cause of their calamity (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">La 3:39</reference>). <div eID="gen17433" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd685e20140d38fd40386dcd61038f1e231cf4e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9839"/><div sID="gen17434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9839"/><hi type="bold">20. tabernacle is spoiled--</hi>metaphor from the tents of nomadic life; as these are taken down in a few moments, so as not to leave a vestige of them, so Judea (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.20">Jr 4:20</reference>).<div eID="gen17434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cords--</hi>with which the coverings of the tent are extended.<div eID="gen17435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">curtains--</hi>tent-curtains. <div eID="gen17436" type="x-p"/>
entries.943d56d6f5c28b4b4330d697d477df77a5b80f8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9840"/><div sID="gen17437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9840"/><hi type="bold">21. pastors--</hi>the rulers, civil and religious. This verse gives the cause of the impending calamity. <div eID="gen17437" type="x-p"/>
entries.666f55d33f70dec407c883472ef045d13ddac1fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9841"/><div sID="gen17438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9841"/><hi type="bold">22. bruit--</hi>rumor of invasion. The antithesis is between the voice of God in His prophets to whom they turned a deaf ear, and the cry of the enemy, a new teacher, whom they must hear [Calvin].<div eID="gen17438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">north country--</hi>Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.15">Jr 1:15</reference>). <div eID="gen17439" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdd96add1ccf79908434e85cfc817485f7cc1cf7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9842"/><div sID="gen17440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9842"/>23. Despairing of influencing the people, he turns to God.<div eID="gen17440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">way of man not in himself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.16.1">Pr 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.24">20:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.13">Jas 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.14">14</reference>). I know, O Jehovah, that the march of the Babylonian conqueror against me (Jeremiah identifying himself with his people) is not at his own discretion, but is overruled by Thee (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.7">Is 10:5-7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.10.19">Jr 10:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that walketh--</hi>when he walketh, that is, sets out in any undertaking.<div eID="gen17442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">direct ... steps--</hi>to give a prosperous issue to (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.23">Psa 73:23</reference>). <div eID="gen17443" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e222c2083c4c1da82d7435e509bdac00fd664e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9843"/><div sID="gen17444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9843"/>24-25. Since I (my nation) must be corrected (justice requiring it because of the deep guilt of the nation), I do not deprecate all chastisement, but pray only for moderation in it (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jr 30:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">Psa 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.1">38:1</reference>); and that the full tide of Thy fury may be poured out on the heathen invaders for their cruelty towards Thy people. <reference osisRef="Ps.79.6">Psa 79:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.7">7</reference>, a psalm to be referred to the time of the captivity, its composer probably repeated this from Jeremiah. The imperative, "Pour out," is used instead of the future, expressing vividly the certainty of the prediction, and that the word of God itself effects its own declarations. Accordingly, the Jews were restored after correction; the Babylonians were utterly extinguished.<div eID="gen17444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know thee ... call ... on thy name--</hi>Knowledge of God is the beginning of piety; calling on Him the fruit.<div eID="gen17445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heathen ... Jacob--</hi>He reminds God of the distinction He has made between His people whom Jacob represents, and the heathen aliens. Correct us as Thy adopted sons, the seed of Jacob; destroy them as outcasts (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.14">Zec 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.21">15, 21</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.10"/>

entries.6c0864361e23a51b99802936bfc93022b121f57d: <div eID="gen29495" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29496" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29497" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29497" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29496" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29498" type="x-p"/> The Jews, about to be carried into captivity, are here warned against the superstition and idolatry of that country to which they were going. Chaldea was greatly addicted to astrology, and therefore the prophet begins with warning them against it, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.1">Jer 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.2">Jer 10:2</reference>. He then exposes the absurdity of idolatry in short but elegant satire; in the midst of which he turns, in a beautiful apostrophe, to the one true God, whose adorable attributes repeatedly strike in view, as he goes along, and lead him to contrast his infinite perfections with those despicable inanities which the blinded nations fear, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.3-Jer.10.16">Jer 10:3-16</reference>. The prophet again denounces the Divine judgments, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.17">Jer 10:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.18">Jer 10:18</reference>; upon which Jerusalem laments her fate, and supplicates the Divine compassion in her favor, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.19-Jer.10.25">Jer 10:19-25</reference>. <div eID="gen29498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29499" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29500" type="x-p"/> Hear ye the word which the Lord speaketh unto you - Dr. Dahler supposes this discourse to have been delivered in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim. It contains an invective against idolatry; showing its absurdity, and that the Creator alone should be worshipped by all mankind.
entries.bcf70154cdc24ac2e3cfdc868049f045ab280fd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29501" type="x-p"/> Learn not the way of the heathen - These words are more particularly addressed to the ten tribes scattered among the heathen by the Assyrians, who carried them away captive; they may also regard those in the land of Israel who still had the customs of the former heathen settlers before their eyes. <div eID="gen29501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29502" type="x-p"/> Be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed - The Chaldeans and Egyptians were notoriously addicated to astrology; and the Israelites here are cautioned against it. The signs of the heavens may mean either the sun, moon, planets, and particular stars or constellations; or the figures or characters by which they represented these heavenly bodies.
entries.cbc466f85b0605eb2a27765e177f175924823e15: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29503" type="x-p"/> The customs of the people are vain - חקות chukkoth; the statutes and principles of the science are vain, empty, and illusory. They are founded in nonsense, ignorance, idolatry, and folly. <div eID="gen29503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29504" type="x-p"/> One cutteth a tree out of the forest - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Isa.40.19">Isa 40:19</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa 44:9</reference> (note), etc., which are all parallel places and where this conduct is strongly ridiculed.
entries.414e98b2b6087cf638e5321ea03f9fb411548d2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29505" type="x-p"/> They are upright as the palm tree - As straight and as stiff as the trees out of which they are hewn.
entries.90c5321f78363f7a8bbe4655b55912e9c8d0143d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29506" type="x-p"/> Who would not fear thee - Who would not worship thee as the Author and Giver of all good? The fear of God is often taken for the whole of true religion. <div eID="gen29506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29507" type="x-p"/> Among all the wise men of the nation - Not even the wisest and most cultivated of the nations have ever found out any one equal to thee; but so exalted and holy art thou, that in all their wisdom and research they have never been able to find out the true God.
entries.e0627efe286f6410623d9c90bf1fab7fc07a8c70: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29508" type="x-p"/> The stock is a doctrine of vanities - Dr. Blayney translates, - "The wood itself is a rebuker of vanities." The very tree out of which the god is hewn demonstrates the vanity and folly of the idolaters; for, can all the art of man make out of a log of wood an animate and intelligent being?
entries.e132b0848ac51af214a39d766df720f19b09375f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29509" type="x-p"/> Brought from Tarshish - Some suppose this to be Tartessus in Spain, from which the Phoenicians brought much silver. Uphaz, Calmet thinks to be the river Pison; some think Ophir is intended. <div eID="gen29509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29510" type="x-p"/> Blue and purple is their clothing - These were the most precious dyes; very rare, and of high price.
entries.6b50117ed4cdd2c7e71db240f575b3332bec4a3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29511" type="x-p"/> But the Lord - The original word should be preserved, however we agree to pronounce it: יהוה Yehovah is the true God. He is without beginning, and without end. This is true of no being else. <div eID="gen29511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29512" type="x-p"/> He is the living God - His being is underived; and he gives life to all. He is the very Fountain whence all life is derived. <div eID="gen29512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29513" type="x-p"/> And an everlasting king - As he has made, so he governs, all things. His sway is felt both in the heavens and in the earth. <div eID="gen29513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29514" type="x-p"/> At his wrath the earth shall tremble - All storms, tempests, tornadoes, and earthquakes are the effects of his power; and when the nations are destroyed, or turned upside down, it is the effect of his displeasure.
entries.44f36434ab1885bf7bb76c2122d46c422778f8ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29515" type="x-p"/> Thus shall ye say unto them - This is the message you shall deliver to the Chaldean idolaters. <div eID="gen29515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29516" type="x-p"/> The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, even they shall perish - Both they and their worshippers shall be destroyed; and idolatry shall finally be destroyed from the earth; and the heavens shall look no more on so great an abomination. It is suffered for a while: but in the end shall be destroyed. This verse is written in a sort of Hebraeo-Syriaco-Chaldee; such a dialect as I suppose was spoken at that time in Babylon, or during the captivity. As it is a message to the Babylonians therefore, it is given in their own language. The Chaldee makes it the beginning of the copy of the epistle which the Prophet Jeremiah sent to the rest of the elders of the captivity who were in Babylon. All the ancient Versions acknowledge this verse; and it is found in all MSS. hitherto collated, except one of Dr. Kennicott's numbered 526; and he has included it between lines, as doubting its authenticity. Dr. Blayney supposes that some public teacher during the captivity, deducing it by direct inference from the prophet's words, had it inserted in the margin, and perhaps usually read together with this section, in the assemblies of the people, in order that they might have their answer always ready, whenever they were molested on the point of religion, or importuned to join the idolatrous worship of the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen29516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29517" type="x-p"/> Dahler has left it entirely out of the text, and introduces it in a note thus: - "After <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10">Jer 10:10</reference> the Hebrew text is interrupted by a verse written in the Chaldean or Babylonish tongue.
